name: Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease)

clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase (PYGL gene) and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, restricting hepatic glycogen breakdown.
Typically presents in early childhood with hepatomegaly and growth restriction, and is generally milder than GSD types I and III.
Fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia is characteristic but is usually mild and better tolerated than in GSD I.
Serum lactate and uric acid are typically normal, a key discriminator from GSD I in which both are raised.
Skeletal and cardiac muscle are spared, distinguishing it from muscle phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease, GSD V).
Transaminases and fasting ketones may be raised, with only mild elevation of triglycerides and cholesterol.
Management centres on avoiding prolonged fasting with frequent carbohydrate-rich meals and uncooked cornstarch, particularly overnight.
Hepatomegaly and biochemical abnormalities often improve with age and around puberty.
reference.pathophysiology: Liver glycogen phosphorylase catalyses the rate-limiting step of hepatic glycogenolysis, cleaving glucose-1-phosphate from the outer branches of glycogen. Loss of function due to PYGL mutations impairs mobilisation of stored hepatic glycogen, so during fasting the liver cannot liberate glucose from glycogen, producing glycogen accumulation with hepatomegaly and a tendency to fasting hypoglycaemia. Because gluconeogenesis and the glucose-6-phosphatase system remain intact and glycolytic flux is preserved, lactate and urate handling are normal and the hypoglycaemia is generally mild and accompanied by ketosis, in clear contrast to GSD I. The affected isoform is liver-specific, so muscle glycogenolysis, which depends on the separate PYGM isoform, is unaffected and there is no myopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Glycogen storage disease type IX (phosphorylase kinase deficiency), which is clinically very similar
Glycogen storage disease type III (debranching enzyme deficiency)
Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke), typically with lactic acidosis and hyperuricaemia
Glycogen storage disease type 0 (hepatic glycogen synthase deficiency)
Fatty acid oxidation defects presenting with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: PYGL molecular genetic testing as the first-line confirmatory test
Controlled fasting studies documenting ketotic hypoglycaemia with normal lactate
Liver biochemistry (transaminases), fasting lipids, lactate and urate
Abdominal ultrasound to assess hepatomegaly and liver texture
Enzyme assay of phosphorylase activity in liver tissue or leucocytes (historical approach)
Phosphorylase kinase assay or genetics to exclude the near-identical GSD IX
redFlags: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or reduced consciousness during intercurrent illness or fasting
Faltering growth or persistent failure to thrive
Progressive hepatomegaly or emerging hepatic fibrosis, which is uncommon but reported
reference.prognosis: The course is generally mild and favourable, with hepatomegaly, growth and biochemical abnormalities tending to normalise with age and dietary management. Serious hepatic complications are uncommon and most affected individuals reach adulthood in good health.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as GSD I; checking lactate and urate, which are normal here, helps distinguish them
Assuming muscle symptoms are needed to consider the diagnosis, when in fact there is no myopathy
Overlooking the almost indistinguishable GSD IX, so molecular testing is needed to separate the two
Attributing mild transaminase elevation to a primary hepatic disease rather than the glycogenosis
references: Saudubray — Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
Scriver — The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Prevent fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia by avoiding prolonged fasts and providing frequent complex-carbohydrate meals and uncooked cornstarch, particularly overnight
Ensure adequate dietary protein to support gluconeogenesis, which remains intact in this disorder
Monitor growth, liver size, transaminases, fasting glucose and ketones, which tend to improve with age
Reassure families given the generally mild course, reserving more intensive intervention for the uncommon significant hypoglycaemia
Distinguish from the near-identical GSD IX and from GSD I so that treatment is appropriately tailored
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive PYGL inheritance with testing of at-risk relatives
